newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan finance chiefs cling to back-room fixer role.
newsitem.headline: Japan finance chiefs cling to back-room fixer role.

text.p: Japanese financial authorities, who started the year with loud proclamations of a new laissez-faire creed, appear lax in practising what they preach when it comes to propping up troubled banks.

Analysts say finance mandarins are clinging closely to their back-room fixer role in orchestrating the restructuring of one of the nation's wobbliest financial institutions with a a plan which would place a burden on stronger, healthier banks.
And that, some critics argue, could be a big mistake.

"The convoy system is still alive and well, and that casts serious doubt on the sincerity with which authorities are looking at the 'Big Bang' (financial reforms) -- or what we thought should be the 'Big Bang,'" said Brian Waterhouse, financial analyst at HSBC James Capel.

Nippon Credit Bank Ltd said last week it expected in early April to unveil a restructuring plan, which banking sources said would include selling real estate and shutting down some overseas operations.
The statement came at a news conference at which a senior bank official denied media reports that a restructuring plan had been mostly worked out.

Banking sources say authorities are considering channelling 80 billion yen ($645 million) in Bank of Japan money, via a fund set up to help wind up failed mortgage firms, to purchase new Nippon Credit shares, which would then be sold to private financial institutions.

The sources also said authorities are asking Japan's top commercial banks to provide about 70 billion yen ($564 million) to buy the new shares and that private financial firms may have to share the burden of losses at three troubled affiliates of Nippon Credit, one of Japan's three long-term credit banks.

Much uncertainty remains over how the final rescue scheme will ultimately play out, but analysts and banking sources said Finance Ministry officials were clearly active in pushing the plan and seeking support from other private banks.

Public pledges as the year began by officials not to intervene to support the tumbling Tokyo stock market were accompanied by private remarks blaming banks for their share of the price slide and urging them to act alone to turn the tide.

Some saw the proclamations as an effort to convince market players that Japan's "Big Bang" financial sector reforms -- a pillar of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's economic platform -- would be accompanied by a change of heart by officials newly willing to let market forces operate freely.

But many analysts doubted both then and now just how committed bureaucrats are to a laissez-faire stance and few expected officials to renege on their promise not to let any of the nation's top 20 banks collapse.

"If you thought the Finance Ministry was really going to leave things to the market, then I've got a bridge to sell you," said one foreign economist. "There was never any intention to wean themselves from intervention. It's business as usual."

In the event, the Tokyo market's key barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, finished the fiscal year on Monday just above the key 18,000 level at 18,003.40 after buying in the final minutes erased about half of the day's earlier plunge.

"It was important to keep the Nikkei above 18,000 to keep Japanese financial institutions slightly above water," said a foreign stock broker. "It's all manipulated, they're up to their same old tricks."
The lower the Nikkei, the greater the erosion of banks' unrealised profits on shareholdings and of their ability to tackle bad debts and stay out of the red.
Banking analysts, meanwhile, warned that the effort to force stronger banks to help out Nippon Credit might backfire, scaring away investors worried the pattern would be repeated.
At the same time, Nippon Credit's restructuring plans could falter on opposition from rival banks, some analysts said.

"This is not allowing market forces to work at all. They are going to run into extreme problems trying to sort it out," Waterhouse said. "I doubt that all major banks have the capacity to join in and those that do, don't want to." ($1=124 yen)
